name: PT Selamat Sempurna Tbk

frontmatter.title: Selamat Sempurna: the filter franchise priced for no growth
frontmatter.summary: Selamat Sempurna makes filters and radiators for the world's replacement market and trades as though that market were shrinking. Nine months of 2026 grew both revenue and profit, the balance sheet carries more cash than debt, and the dividend is already declared. We stay at BUY with a lower target of Rp2,649, 73.0% above the last traded price, after working capital is anchored on the September 2026 actual.
thesis: The franchise is the aftermarket, not the car makers: 85.0% of revenue is recurring aftermarket revenue and the product reaches 125 countries, so a weak new-car market does not stop the top line [S4, S3].

The price assumes no growth: at our cost of capital Rp1,620 needs revenue to shrink in every year from FY2026E, -5.6% a year at the point the solver reports, against the 6.5% we forecast for FY2027E [S0, S2].
The balance sheet is the floor: cash of 1,173.4 against debt of 173.0, capex at 3.6% of revenue and a return on equity of 30.9% [S5, S3].
Cash returns are committed: more than two decades of annual dividend increases, a 72.0% payout on FY2025 profit and a third interim of Rp45.0/share already declared for 2026 [S4, S7].
The risk is a dollar export book that is already shrinking and a rupiah that stops helping, which is the bear case at Rp2,303 rather than our base case at Rp2,622 [S3, S4].

blocks.text: We maintain coverage of PT Selamat Sempurna Tbk with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp2,649, which is 73.0% above the Rp1,620 at which the shares last traded [S0]. This revision brings the model onto the third-quarter 2026 data pack and the nine-month filing to 30 September 2026, and it changes three things. The quarter itself produced no revision on the top line: revenue and profit for the nine months are the figures the forecast was already built on [S2, S4]. The working-capital ratio is now anchored on the September balance sheet rather than on the prior year-end, which lowers the target, and the fourth quarter is now carried at the observed seasonal ratios rather than at a discount to them, which raises it; the net is a target slightly below the previous version, and the rating is unchanged [S2, S0]. The balance sheet is carried at 30 September 2026 inside the data pack rather than at 30 June, so the roll-forward adjustment the previous version made for the June-to-September fall in net cash has been removed to avoid counting that fall twice [S2, S0]. The company manufactures filters and radiators for the replacement market, sells them into more than a hundred countries under its own brands, and is the largest filter maker in the region by its own description [S4]. It is not a car-parts supplier in the usual sense: 85.0% of revenue is recurring aftermarket revenue, so the buyer is a distributor or a workshop replacing a worn part rather than a vehicle assembler negotiating an annual price down [S4].

The disagreement with the price is about the durability of that annuity, not about the next quarter. At Rp1,620 the shares trade at 7.6x our FY2026E earnings and 4.8x EBITDA, with a forward dividend yield of 9.5% and net cash on the balance sheet [S0]. A reverse DCF on our own cost of capital says the price is only justified if a single growth shock of -12.1% is applied to every forecast year, taking FY2026E growth from our 8.3% to below zero and FY2027E, the year the solver reports, to -5.6% — a business that shrinks permanently rather than one that grows at the 6.5% we forecast [S0, S2]. The nine months of 2026 do not describe a stalling business: revenue rose 6.7% and parent net profit 6.7%, with the third quarter accelerating [S4, S2].

Three things move the value from here. The first is whether the export book stabilises in dollars: overseas sales are the larger half of the mix, they grew only 1.6% in rupiah over the nine months while the rupiah ran well above its FY2025A average, and the domestic line at 16.2% carried the growth off a weak base [S4, S0]. The second is the gross margin: it has held in a narrow band through a rupiah that moved from Rp15,846/USD to Rp18,012/USD, and the question is whether that pass-through survives a year in which input costs fall and customers ask for the saving back [S5, S2]. The third is capital return, where the record is unusually strong and the policy floor is far below what the company actually pays [S3, S4].

Filters and radiators are consumables disguised as components. A filter is replaced several times over a vehicle's life, the part number is specified by the original equipment maker, and the buyer chooses on availability and brand trust rather than on the price of the part alone. That gives an incumbent with a deep catalogue and a wide distributor network a structural advantage: the catalogue is expensive to replicate, the distributor already carries the stock, and a workshop will not risk a cheap filter on a customer's engine. Radiators are slower-moving and more exposed to new-vehicle production, which is why the filter line carries the franchise and the body-maker and trading lines are cyclical attachments to it.

PT Selamat Sempurna Tbk is the flagship of the ADR Group's automotive division and describes itself as the largest filter manufacturer in the region, with the most comprehensive product range of any auto-component company it competes with [S4]. It makes filtration products for automotive, commercial-vehicle, heavy-equipment, marine and industrial applications, and heat-exchange products that include copper-brass, aluminium-plastic and all-aluminium radiators, condensers, intercoolers and evaporators [S4]. The catalogue runs to about 10,000 part numbers and the company adds roughly 300 part numbers a year, which is the engine of the aftermarket franchise rather than a marketing line [S4].

The segment mix is filter-led and becoming more so. In FY2025 the filter segment sold 4,058 IDR bn of the group total, radiators 592 IDR bn, the trading and distribution arm 1,659 IDR bn and body maker 144 IDR bn, with other products and eliminations making up the difference [S3]. In the nine months of 2026 the filter line contributed 2,985 IDR bn, radiators 489 IDR bn, trading 1,415 IDR bn and body maker 157 IDR bn, so the filter share of the business is stable and the body-maker line remains small after falling 45.9% in FY2025 [S4, S3]. Trading is a distribution business that sells third-party parts alongside the group's own, which is why its revenue is large relative to its profit and why the segment table eliminates a quarter of gross sales on consolidation [S3].

Manufacturing sits at two sites in Indonesia, Kapuk in Jakarta for heat exchange and Tangerang in Banten for filtration and other products, plus a filtration plant in Klang, Malaysia [S4]. Capacity is 115 m pcs of filters a year and 1.9 m units of radiators, against FY2025 production of 82.7 m units filters and 834 k units radiators, so utilisation is roughly three quarters in filters and well under half in radiators [S4, S3]. That spare capacity matters for the forecast: growth to FY2030E needs working capital and debottlenecking rather than a new plant, which is why capex stays near 3.4% of revenue [S3, S4].

The customer base is global and the channel is replacement. The company exports to 125 countries and holds trademark registrations in more than a hundred and thirty, and it describes 85.0% of revenue as recurring aftermarket revenue [S4]. In FY2025 overseas sales were 3,450 IDR bn, up 10.7%, while consolidated domestic sales fell 7.8%, so the export book carried the year while the domestic market contracted [S3]. The nine months of 2026 reversed that pattern, with domestic sales up 16.2% and overseas up 1.6%, which is the first evidence in two years that the Indonesian aftermarket is recovering [S4].

Control sits with PT Adrindo Intiperkasa, which held 50.5% of the 5,759 m shares at 30 September 2026, with the remainder held by institutions and individuals and a public float of 49.5% [S4]. The company is not part of a conglomerate group in the house registry, so no konglo lens applies. Management's stated strategy is to defend the aftermarket position in commercial vehicles and heavy-duty applications, diversify the export base, and add part numbers rather than capacity, which is consistent with a business that earns its return on catalogue breadth rather than on asset turns [S3].

The industry the company sells into is the global automotive replacement market, and the relevant demand driver is the vehicle parc rather than new-vehicle sales. That distinction is the whole investment case. Indonesian domestic car sales were 803,687 units in 2025, down 7.2%, on weak purchasing power and tighter vehicle financing, and the annual report is explicit that the entry-level segment was under the most pressure while commercial vehicles held up better [S3]. A parts supplier selling to the assemblers would have had a poor year. Selamat Sempurna grew revenue 3.4% because the cars already on the road still need filters [S3].

The macro backdrop the company describes is one of moderate global growth, trade fragmentation and geopolitical risk. The annual report cites the IMF's projection of about 3.1% global growth for 2026, notes that global monetary policy is turning more accommodative but cautiously, and flags the Middle East and the Strait of Hormuz as a risk to energy prices, logistics costs and distribution [S3]. Indonesia itself grew 5.1% in 2025, which supported domestic demand even as car sales fell [S3]. The company's own 2026 outlook is cautious: it expects the automotive and component industry to keep developing in a careful environment, with commercial-vehicle demand tied to real-sector activity and financing conditions [S3].

Competition in filters is fragmented at the low end and concentrated at the branded end. The company's position rests on three things it states directly: the breadth of the range, the number of part numbers, and the export footprint [S4]. Those are switching costs of a particular kind. A distributor carrying ten thousand part numbers has working capital tied up in the relationship and a catalogue its customers rely on, and a workshop that fits a filter by part number has little reason to test a cheaper alternative on a customer's engine. The moat is therefore distribution and catalogue depth rather than a patent or a cost advantage, and it is strongest in the commercial-vehicle and heavy-duty aftermarket where the company says it is positioned [S3].

The five forces read as follows. Buyer power is moderate: distributors are large but fragmented, and the end buyer is a consumer of a low-ticket part. Supplier power is moderate and rising with steel and media prices, though the company buys in dollars against dollar revenue, which nets much of the exposure. New entrants face a catalogue and certification barrier in the branded aftermarket but can enter the low-end domestic market, which is where price competition lives. Substitutes are limited, because a filter is a consumable with a service interval. Rivalry is the main force, and it is expressed through discounting in the domestic trade rather than through capacity wars, because the industry's capacity is already built [S3, S4].

The external influences that matter are the rupiah, steel and filter-media prices, freight, and trade policy in the export markets. The house macro deck carries the rupiah at Rp18,012/USD spot, Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E and Rp19,000/USD in the long run, against an FY2025A average of Rp16,448/USD: the deck expects further depreciation, not stability [S0]. The translation effect is already in the numbers we are forecasting from, which is the point the previous version missed. With 62.0% of revenue overseas and priced in dollars, overseas sales rose only 1.6% in rupiah over the nine months while the rupiah ran well above its FY2025A average of Rp16,448/USD; in dollars the export book therefore shrank, and the group's rupiah growth came from the domestic line at 16.2% [S4, S2, S0]. Two conclusions follow. First, a weaker rupiah is an arithmetic tailwind to reported rupiah revenue and to EBITDA in rupiah, but it is not evidence of volume growth, and we do not add a second translation layer on top of a forecast whose base year already contains one. Second, the offsetting cost side is real: the filing shows the majority of third-party trade payables denominated in foreign currency, which is the visible sign of a dollar-linked input base, so a matched cost base absorbs most of the translation at the gross-margin line rather than lifting it [S2]. We therefore exclude FX as a separate base-case line and say so explicitly: the currency split of cost of goods sold is not disclosed, so any net figure would be an assumption, and the margin's stability through a rupiah that moved from Rp15,846/USD to Rp18,012/USD is the evidence that the offset is close to complete [S5, S2]. The currency enters through the scenarios instead, as a softer rupiah in the bull case and, in the bear, through imported competing parts undercutting domestic prices rather than through our cost line [S4, S3]. Trade fragmentation is the less quantifiable risk: unilateral tariffs and regional content rules can redirect the export book, and the annual report names them as a factor in the 2025 environment [S3].

The global filtration aftermarket is structurally attractive because the installed base of vehicles, trucks and industrial equipment keeps growing even in years when new sales fall, and because service intervals are set by engine manufacturers rather than by the part supplier. The industry's economics reward catalogue breadth and logistics density: a distributor that can fill a mixed order from one warehouse wins the workshop's business, and a manufacturer that can supply that breadth at a competitive landed cost wins the distributor. This is why the large filtration names in most regions are decades-old franchises with thousands of part numbers rather than recent entrants, and why consolidation in the sector has historically been about buying catalogues rather than buying plants.

The historical record is one of steady top-line growth and a margin that has improved through the cycle. Revenue went from 4,894.2 in FY2022A to 5,338.8 in FY2025A, a compound rate in the low single digits over three years, while the gross margin rose from 32.8% to 37.1% and the EBIT margin from 22.5% to 28.1% [S0, S5]. The improvement is not a single-year artefact: it survived a rupiah that moved from Rp14,843/USD to Rp16,448/USD and a rise in input costs, which is the strongest evidence that the company prices through its cost base rather than absorbing it [S5, S3].

The FY2025 accounts are the anchor for the forecast. Revenue was 5,338.8, cost of goods sold 3,360.6, gross profit 1,978.1 and operating profit 1,502.2, with selling expenses of 305 IDR bn and general and administrative expenses of 237 IDR bn [S5]. The operating line is flattered by other operating income, which is why the model's opex ratio is struck net of it: the reported operating profit of 1,502.2 is gross profit less selling and G&A plus other operating income, and the ratio that matters for the forecast is the net figure of 9.1% of revenue [S5, S2].

The nine months of 2026 are the more important evidence because they are the most recent and they are audited-adjacent. Revenue was 4,183 IDR bn, gross profit 1,533 IDR bn and operating profit 1,172 IDR bn, with profit attributable to the owners of the parent of 874 IDR bn and group profit of 958 IDR bn after 84.3 IDR bn to non-controlling interests [S2]. The gross margin of 37.0% and operating margin of 28.0% are consistent with the full-year history, and the net margin of 21.0% is in line with the 21.1% the company earned on parent profit in FY2025A rather than above it [S6, S2, S5]. Our FY2026E revenue of 5,780.3 is built from the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the FY2025 observed Q4/Q3 revenue ratio, not from a growth assumption [S2, S4].

Measured against the forecast we published, the third quarter is on track rather than a surprise in either direction. Nine-month revenue of 4,183 IDR bn is 6.7% up on the prior-year period, and because our FY2026E of 5,780.3 was struck from these actuals plus a fourth quarter at the third quarter's run rate, the quarter delivered the run rate the model already carries: the acceleration we flagged in the prior version is the third quarter's, and it has not been revised [S2, S4]. On the profit lines the comparison is the same: nine-month parent profit of 874 IDR bn is 6.7% higher, our FY2026E parent profit is 1,228.2 and earnings per share 213.3, and the nine months therefore carry the great majority of the full-year number with only the fourth quarter to come [S2, S0]. The one line where the filing moved the model is the balance sheet: cash of 943 IDR bn and time deposits of 116 IDR bn against bank loans and lease facilities leave the group in net cash, and that position is now captured at the 30 September date itself rather than through an adjustment [S2, S0]. This revision changes four assumptions, each to move the model onto the latest actual rather than away from it. FY2026E growth moves up to 8.3% because the fourth quarter is now carried at the observed FY2025 Q4/Q3 ratio; the FY2026E gross margin moves up to 37.8% because the fourth quarter is carried at the margin the FY2025 fourth quarter actually earned; and the working-capital ratio moves up to 43.1% because that is the ratio on the 30 September balance sheet [S2, S5, S0]. The revenue path after FY2026E is unchanged, because the capacity arithmetic that drives the taper has not changed [S3, S4].

The earnings-quality picture is mixed and it deteriorated year on year, which is worth stating plainly rather than leaving in the accruals gap. Operating cash flow in the nine months was 591 IDR bn against group profit of 958 IDR bn, and the same comparison a year earlier was 744 IDR bn against 889 IDR bn: cash flow fell while profit rose, so the cash conversion rate dropped sharply [S2]. The cash-flow statement shows where the cash went, and it is not a mystery. Cash received from customers rose from 3,815 IDR bn to 4,053 IDR bn, about as fast as revenue, while cash paid to suppliers rose from 2,151 IDR bn to 2,535 IDR bn and other taxes paid from 16.3 IDR bn to 44.8 IDR bn: the supplier line alone absorbed more cash than the customer line added, which is what a working-capital build looks like from the payment side [S2]. The balance-sheet cause is the same one flagged below: inventories of 1,610 IDR bn against 1,250 IDR bn at the prior year-end while cost of goods sold was 2,650 IDR bn, and third-party trade receivables of 1,305 IDR bn against 1,173 IDR bn [S2]. Some of it is defensible, because a business that adds part numbers and serves 125 countries carries breadth in stock, but the direction is a use of cash and it is why our working-capital ratio is the one on the September balance sheet, 43.1% of revenue, held flat rather than assumed to unwind [S2].

The consequence for the forecast is arithmetically demanding and we do not hide it. The model's FY2026E free cash flow of 828.5 sits against nine-month operating cash flow of 591 IDR bn and capex of 93.4 IDR bn, so the fourth quarter has to deliver the balance of the year's cash after a nine-month conversion of about two thirds of profit — better than anything the nine months produced, though not out of line with the FY2025 fourth quarter, when the seasonal mix is at its richest [S2, S5]. We carry that requirement as a named risk in section five rather than as an assumption we can source.

Receivables are the second divergence and the one we had under-weighted. Third-party trade receivables rose to 1,305 IDR bn from 1,173 IDR bn while revenue grew 6.7%, a ratio of more than one and a half times revenue growth, which is the trigger in our earnings-quality card and works out at about a quarter of a year of sales outstanding [S2]. The filing states that the group carries no significant concentration of credit risk, so this is not a single-customer problem, but it is a second channel of the same kind as the inventory build, and the two together are why the working-capital ratio is the largest single user of cash in the forecast [S2]. Our base case holds the September ratio flat, because neither the filing nor the IR deck states a year-end unwind; the bear case has both channels still building, which takes the ratio above the September level rather than below it [S2, S4].

The second flag is the cost line. Selling expenses rose to 286 IDR bn and G&A to 163 IDR bn, both faster than revenue, and the operating line was supported by other operating income of 147 IDR bn against a much smaller figure a year earlier [S2]. That is not a sustainable source of margin, and our forecast does not extrapolate it. Nor do we assume the ratio improves: measured against the prior-year period rather than the full year, the nine-month opex ratio was worse, not better, and no cost programme is disclosed in the filing, the annual report or the IR deck, so the ratio is held flat at the FY2026E level to the end of the forecast [S2, S3, S4]. The third flag is related-party purchasing, which was 8.5% of consolidated cost of goods sold in the nine months, with related-party sales of 58.7 IDR bn [S2]. That is disclosed, priced and stable against the prior year, but it is a governance item we return to in section six.

Cash conversion and the balance sheet are the counterweight. Operating cash flow in FY2025 was 1,124 IDR bn against capital expenditure of 136 IDR bn on the cash-flow statement, and the company held 1,173.4 of cash against 173.0 of debt, so the group is in net cash [S5]. At 30 September 2026 cash was 943 IDR bn with 116 IDR bn of time deposits against bank loans and lease liabilities that leave the group in net cash, and total equity had risen to 4,636 IDR bn [S2]. The company funds its dividend from operating cash flow and still adds to cash, which is the definition of a business that does not need the capital markets [S5, S2].

Capital allocation is unusually shareholder-friendly for an Indonesian industrial. Dividends paid were 806 IDR bn in FY2025 and 605 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026, the latter including the final dividend for FY2025 paid in July [S5, S2]. On capex we use one measure throughout: cash-flow purchases plus advances for fixed assets, which put FY2025 spend above depreciation of 182.3, with the annual report stating realised capital expenditure of 205 IDR bn against a similar figure in 2024 [S5, S3, S4]. The asset base is therefore being maintained and modestly expanded rather than sweated, and the long-run ratio is held near the current 3.6% of revenue because the spend is maintenance-led and the plant carries utilisation headroom in radiators, not because the asset base is shrinking [S3, S4]. The forecast holds capex there and lets cash build, which is why the net cash position widens every year in the model [S0].

Our forecast is a continuation, not a recovery or a fade. Revenue grows 8.3% in FY2026E, then 6.5%, 5.5%, 5.0% and 4.5%, with a 4.0% long run [S0]. The taper is a capacity calculation rather than caution: filter production of 82.7 m units against 110 m units of capacity leaves about a quarter of headroom, and at the growth rates above the filter line approaches full utilisation inside the forecast, after which volume needs new plant; the radiator line at 834 k units produced against 1.9 m units of capacity is where the spare capacity sits [S3, S4]. The gross margin is 37.8% in FY2026E — the nine-month actual lifted by the fourth quarter carried at the margin the FY2025 fourth quarter actually earned — and 37.0% thereafter, the last audited full-year level, so no part of the value depends on holding an expanded margin for a decade [S2, S5]. The opex ratio is held at 9.1% and the tax rate at 20.0% [S2, S5]. On those inputs profit attributable to the owners reaches 1,228.2 in FY2026E and earnings per share 213.3, a return on equity of 30.6% [S0]. For scale on the two corrections in this revision: the fourth-quarter seasonality is worth a few rupiah per share in total, and each point of revenue growth is worth about one per cent of the target, so neither changes the rating [S0].

We value the company on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with P/E and EV/EBITDA as cross-checks, which is the house method set for the auto-components industry and the right one here. The business generates free cash flow to the firm of 910.8 on revenue of 5,338.8, converts most of its profit into cash, and carries net cash rather than debt, so a cash-flow method captures what an owner actually receives [S5]. The multiple methods are the cross-check because the peer set is a mix of assemblers, component makers and distributors with very different capital structures, and a single multiple would import their leverage into our value [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck and the build has to be shown in full, because one step in it is easy to miss. The starting point is the ten-year Indonesian government yield of 7.4%, from which the house method subtracts the sovereign default spread of 1.6%: a government bond yield is not a risk-free rate in a country with default risk, and leaving the spread in would charge the same premium twice, once in the base rate and again in the country risk premium. The base rate is therefore 7.4% less 1.6%; adding 0.91 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesian country premium of 2.5% gives a cost of equity of 11.9% [S0]. The levered beta is the industry unlevered beta of 0.90 geared for a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.02, and with debt at 1.5% of the capital structure at a pre-tax cost of 9.4% the weighted average cost of capital is 11.9% [S0]. Read without the default-spread step the same inputs would give a rate above the house band for an Indonesian industrial; with it, 11.9% is inside the band, and the terminal growth of 4.0% is below the long-run nominal growth of the economy [S0]. The rate matters: against a base DCF of Rp3,007 a share, one point more on the cost of capital takes the grid to about two thousand seven hundred, eleven per cent lower, and one point less to about three thousand four hundred, fourteen per cent higher — between a ninth and a seventh, the larger effect on the way down because a lower rate lengthens the perpetuity — and on the DCF's half weight that is about five to seven per cent of the blended target; both ends are visible in the sensitivity grid below [S0].

The DCF produces a value of Rp3,007 per share, with the terminal value at 50.5% of the total, which is a normal shape for a business with a long growth runway and modest capital intensity [S0]. The explicit forecast carries free cash flow from 828.5 in FY2026E to 1,792.8 in FY2035E. The net cash position is added to the enterprise value and the minority interest of 533 IDR bn at 30 September 2026 is deducted — the same balance-sheet date the cash figure comes from, and not the prior year-end balance — which is the correct bridge for a group that consolidates a Malaysian subsidiary it does not wholly own; the only post-period item is the third interim dividend, already inside the modelled payout [S2, S7].

A terminal value struck on a growth rate is still a multiple in disguise, so we run the survival test rather than let the formula hide it. On FY2035E the terminal value implies an exit multiple above the 4.8x at which the shares change hands today, and above the company's own four-observation average. We state that plainly: half the DCF's value rests on an exit multiple richer than today's price. The question the method card asks is whether a rational buyer would pay that exit multiple, and on the fundamentals we think it would, because the terminal year still earns a return on equity of 22.3% against a cost of equity of 11.9%; a buyer paying that multiple for those returns, on a business that grows at 4.0%, is not paying for optimism, though the caveat in the next paragraph is that a working-capital-only reinvestment flatters that return. The anomaly is the entry multiple, not the exit. As a check, had we struck the terminal value at today's entry multiple instead of the perpetuity, the DCF would fall by roughly a quarter and still sit above the price.

A perpetuity on a growth rate is a statement about reinvestment and return, so the two have to be stated together. In FY2035E the model reinvests 143.7, all of it working capital, because capex of 294.8 equals depreciation of 294.8 and there is no net fixed-capital investment in the terminal year; against operating profit of 2,420.7 taxed at 20.0% that leaves free cash flow of 1,792.8, so the retention rate is the working-capital build divided by after-tax operating profit — about seven per cent — and the 4.0% terminal growth divided by that retention rate is the return on incremental capital the perpetuity embeds, about fifty-four per cent, several times the 11.9% we discount at [S0]. The earlier version of this paragraph left both ratios unstated and the red team computed about sixty per cent from the same block; the difference between that figure and ours is arithmetic, not mechanism, because the growth-path revision in this version moved the terminal year's revenue and therefore lifted the working-capital build and the taxed profit together, so the pair now sits at roughly seven and fifty-four rather than the higher retention and return struck on the earlier path [S0]. Those are the two numbers the compounder card asks for, and neither is defended as a forecast of the terminal year alone. That is a high number and it is the single assumption in this valuation most open to challenge, so here is the mechanism rather than a defence. Growth at 4.0% in this business is catalogue and aftermarket volume, and the capacity is already bought: filter production of 82.7 m units against 110 m units of capacity and radiator production of 834 k units against 1.9 m units mean the next several years of volume come from debottlenecking, not from a new plant, and the marginal capital they need is stock and receivables [S3, S4]. The historical record is the same: revenue grew while capex of 3.6% of revenue ran close to a depreciation charge of 182.3 on revenue of 5,338.8, which is growth financed out of working capital and maintenance rather than out of new capital [S5, S3]. What we cannot do in this engine is run an explicit two-stage fade, because the terminal value is a single-stage perpetuity; the fade is therefore carried in the growth path, which steps from 8.3% to 4.5% to 4.0%, and in the margin, which reverts to the last audited level rather than holding the FY2026E mix. We state the limit openly: once utilisation closes, incremental volume does need plant, the incremental return falls toward the cost of capital, and the perpetuity would be worth less. The sensitivity grid prices that risk directly — the corner that cuts terminal growth by a point and adds a point to the cost of capital, the furthest step in each direction the grid carries, puts the DCF about fifteen per cent below base and is the closest the engine gets to a fade to cost of capital, and it is the honest downside bound on this method [S0].

The moat that justifies carrying the growth as long as we do is distribution and catalogue depth — 10,000 part numbers across filters and radiators, 300 part numbers added a year, sold into 125 countries — which is a switching-cost moat of the working-capital kind rather than a patent. The evidence that it is holding rather than widening is that the filter line grew 1.4% in the nine months while Indonesian car sales fell 7.2% in 2025; the evidence against is that filters lagged group revenue growth, which is exactly why we fade the growth rate rather than extend it [S4, S3].

The cross-checks sit below the DCF and we do not smooth the difference away. The P/E method values the shares at Rp2,003 on a multiple of 10.3, which is the average of the peer median and the company's own mean over the four annual observations the data pack carries — not five, which is the label we used before — and it is -33.4% below the DCF [S0]. The EV/EBITDA method gives Rp1,878 at 6.2, -37.5% below the DCF, and it is run on the restated FY2025A EBITDA of 1,684.5, not on the data pack's un-restated figure, which is built on a depreciation charge far below the audited accounts [S3, S5]. The own-history benchmark inside that multiple is itself still computed on the pack's un-restated history, which pushes the benchmark up by roughly the same proportion as the metric was pushed down; restating both would leave the method within a few per cent of where it stands, so the two errors largely offset and we disclose them rather than adjust one side only [S0, S3]. The gap to the DCF is then informative rather than embarrassing: the peer median multiple is dragged down by assemblers and by component makers with weaker returns, while the company earns a return on equity of 30.9% and pays out most of its profit, which a cash-flow method captures and a peer multiple does not [S0, S5].

One convention needs stating because it is a real inconsistency, not a judgment. The DCF is struck at the valuation date on forward cash flows and then rolled forward a year at the cost of equity to produce the twelve-month target, while both multiples apply a benchmark to the last audited year's earnings. The cross-checks are therefore trailing against a forward primary, which biases the blend down; on FY2026E metrics the same benchmarks would value the shares higher and the target would be a few per cent above the published figure. We keep the trailing convention because it rests on audited numbers a reader can verify, and we flag the direction of the bias rather than adjust it away.

The blend weights the DCF at 50%, P/E at 30% and EV/EBITDA at 20%, which produces a fundamental value of Rp2,480 before the roll-forward [S0]. The base-scenario twelve-month target is Rp2,622; the published target of Rp2,649 is the probability-weighted average of the three scenarios at half base and a quarter each to bear and bull, and it sits slightly above the base-scenario target rather than below it [S0]. We say plainly why the weighted figure is the higher one: the shocks are mirrored, but a DCF is convex in the growth rate, so the bull's gain on three points of growth, one and a half points of margin and three points of working-capital release is larger than the bear's equal-and-opposite loss; the asymmetry is arithmetic, not a tilted probability set or a discretionary uplift [S0]. The target is 73.0% above the last price, and the sensitivity grid shows how much of that depends on the two inputs we are least certain about, revenue growth and the gross margin, and how much on the discount rate [S0]. Read from the grid rather than asserted: two points of gross margin move the twelve-month value from about two thousand five hundred to about two thousand seven hundred and forty, four and a half per cent either way, or about two and a quarter per cent a point. One point of the cost of capital moves the DCF from Rp3,007 to about two thousand seven hundred when the rate is a point higher, eleven per cent down, and about three thousand four hundred when it is a point lower, fourteen per cent up, and at the DCF's 50% weight that is about five to seven per cent of the blended target — more than the four and a half per cent that two points of gross margin are worth. The rate is therefore the more powerful single input, not the less, and the earlier version of this paragraph had the comparison the wrong way round; we withdraw it rather than defend it. That ordering is worth stating because the rate is inherited from the house deck rather than forecast from the company [S0, S5].

What the price implies is the most useful number in this section, and it should be quoted the way the engine solves it rather than smoothed. The reverse DCF applies a single shock of -12.1% to our revenue growth in every forecast year: FY2026E becomes our 8.3% less that shock, FY2027E our 6.5% less it, FY2030E our 4.5% less it, and FY2031E onwards the 4.0% long run less it — the solver's binding year, FY2027E, lands at -5.6% [S0]. The terminal value is then capitalised at the unchanged 4.0%, which means the solved path is a shrinking explicit period that jumps back to growth in perpetuity; that discontinuity is a property of the solver and we state it rather than describe the path as a smooth taper. Read the other way, holding our growth path and the 4.0% terminal growth, the price would require a discount rate materially above the 11.9% we use; the engine solves growth only and we do not run a reverse cost-of-capital solve, so we state that direction and quote no rate rather than derive one by hand. Either reading says the same thing: the market is not forecasting a collapse in the business, it is applying a discount rate we cannot reproduce from the fundamentals. We therefore name the mechanisms rather than assert a gap. PT Adrindo Intiperkasa holds 50.5% of the shares, the public — every holder outside the controlling block — holds 49.5%, and foreign institutions account for 25.1%; the shares turn over about IDR5.6bn a day, the stock carries no high-concentration listing and no conglomerate affiliation in the house registry, and 62.0% of revenue is exported into a tariff environment the annual report names as a risk [S4, S0, S3]. A liquidity and governance discount of that order is real and we do not argue it away; what we cannot source is a discount of the size this price implies.

The nine-month actuals do not support the contraction either. Revenue grew 6.7%, net profit 6.7%, the third quarter accelerated, and the company has raised its dividend for twenty-one consecutive years [S4, S2]. We accept that this pack contains no scenario that reaches the market price, and we say so in section five rather than invent one: the gap between our worst case and the price is a statement about the discount rate, not about the earnings.

The first risk is that the export book is weaker than the rupiah numbers make it look. Overseas sales are the larger half of the mix and grew only 1.6% in the nine months while the rupiah ran well above its FY2025A average of Rp16,448/USD, so in dollars the export line fell; the group's growth came from the domestic line at 16.2% off a weak base, and the third quarter's acceleration is a rupiah figure that mixes volume with translation [S4, S2, S0]. If the domestic line decelerates while the export book stays flat in dollars, revenue growth falls toward the bear case, and the operating leverage in a business with a 9.1% opex ratio works in reverse [S2].

The second risk is the currency, and we state it in the direction the evidence supports rather than the direction that reads well. 62.0% of nine-month revenue is overseas, so the revenue side is substantially dollar-linked; the filings do not disclose the currency split of cost of goods sold, so we cannot net the cost side from the accounts, and we therefore do not model a rupiah shock at all. The reason is not indifference: the base year already contains a translation gain from a much weaker rupiah, so a second translation layer would double-count, and section two sets out why the dollar input base makes the net margin effect small [S0, S2]. What a weaker rupiah does unambiguously is make imported competing parts cheaper in rupiah terms and compress the domestic margin, so the currency reaches the bear through the same domestic-discounting channel as competition, not as a separate cost mechanism [S4, S3].

The third risk is the domestic car market. Indonesian car sales fell 7.2% in 2025 and the annual report attributes the fall to purchasing power and vehicle financing [S3]. A second weak year would not stop the aftermarket, but it would keep the body-maker and trading lines under pressure, and the body-maker segment has already fallen 45.9% [S3]. The fourth risk is governance and liquidity: a 50.5% controlling shareholder, a public float of 49.5% and a related-party purchase ratio of 8.5% of cost of goods sold are all facts an owner should price, even when the related-party terms are disclosed and stable [S4, S2].

The fifth risk is competitive discounting in the domestic aftermarket. The company's advantage is catalogue and distribution, not a cost advantage, and a competitor with a narrower range can always undercut on a specific part number [S4]. The sixth is input cost: steel, filter media and freight are the cost base, and the annual report names energy and raw-material prices as a 2026 risk alongside trade fragmentation [S3]. The seventh, new in this revision, is cash conversion. Nine-month operating cash flow of 591 IDR bn compares with 744 IDR bn a year earlier while profit rose, so the conversion rate has fallen sharply, and the forecast needs a fourth quarter that delivers most of the year's cash [S2]. The sensitivity grid does not carry a conversion row, so we size it directly: the working-capital ratio the forecast uses is the September actual, and every three points on that ratio is the difference between the base and the bear [S0, S2]. None of these is a thesis-breaker on its own; the bear case combines a demand reversal, domestic discounting and a working-capital build, which is why the three shocks are applied together rather than one at a time [S0, S2].

The bear case assumes revenue growth three percentage points lower in every year, a gross margin one and a half points lower on domestic discounting, and a working-capital ratio three points higher as inventory and receivables both keep building, which takes it above the September level rather than below it [S3, S4, S2]. It values the shares at Rp2,303, still above the current price, because the starting point is a business with net cash, a 11.9% cost of capital and a dividend that covers a large part of the return [S0]. We do not hide that: no scenario in this pack reaches Rp1,620, and section four says why — the price is not discounting our bear case, it is discounting at a rate above anything we can build from this company's fundamentals. If that discount persists, the shares can stay where they are while the business performs; that de-rating risk is the real risk a buyer takes here, and it cannot be expressed as an earnings shock without inventing a collapse the filings do not support.

The bull case assumes the aftermarket share gain accelerates, with the radiator line filling spare capacity — production of 834 k units against 1.9 m units of capacity — and the body-maker line, already up 40.5% in the nine months, holding its recovery, alongside input costs easing and a softer rupiah against a dollar revenue base [S4, S3]. It carries growth three points higher, the margin one and a half points higher and working capital releasing, which values the shares at Rp3,046 [S0, S4]. On the radiators, the earlier version of this report called the fill a fraction of a growth point and that was wrong, so here is the arithmetic from the disclosure: 489 IDR bn of nine-month sales for 845 k units units against a capacity of 1.9 m units means the line could roughly double its volume, which annualised is of the order of a tenth of group revenue [S4]. That is a real lever, not a rounding error. It is nonetheless inside the three-point growth shock, because that shock is applied to every year of the forecast and compounds, while a one-off fill is a level shift that then grows with the base; the two are the same order of present value and the growth shock is the broader of the two, so we do not stack a separate volume shock on top of it [S0, S4].

On capital return we size the surplus rather than assert it. Cash on the balance sheet rises from 1,173.4 to 2,479.3 by FY2030E, against net debt that is negative throughout, while the model still pays out 72.0%, so the group accumulates distributable cash every year. We do not add a special dividend on top of that, and the reason is method rather than caution: the valuation discounts cash flows before financing, so paying the surplus out would change the mix between cash and distributions but not enterprise value, and the surplus is counted once, at the last balance-sheet date, through the bridge. The same mechanics mean the cash the business builds after the forecast starts is not capitalised at all, so this channel is a conservative element in our value rather than an aggressive one. Payout is deliberately not a scenario shock, and the earlier version was wrong to make it one. In an enterprise-value DCF the payout changes only the split between dividend and balance-sheet cash, not the discounted cash flows, so the only channel it has is the dividend subtracted in the twelve-month roll-forward — which means a cut mechanically raises the target and a raise lowers it, the opposite of what the narrative says. We have therefore removed it from the bear and the bull and treat it as an income-versus-capital choice: the same value, paid out or retained [S0].

The base case at Rp2,622 carries half the probability and the weighted target of Rp2,649 sits just above it: on mirrored shocks the bull's gain is larger than the bear's loss, so the probability weighting lifts the target rather than pulling it down, and the bear is a slowdown rather than a collapse [S0].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. Two consecutive quarters in which overseas sales fall in dollars while the domestic line slows would tell us the growth was a rupiah effect and a weak-base recovery rather than volume, and we would cut the growth path toward the bear. A gross margin below the bottom of the recent band for a full year would tell us the pass-through has broken, and we would cut the margin input rather than wait for a recovery. A related-party purchase ratio that rises materially above its current level, or a change in the controlling shareholder's stake, would be a governance signal we would treat as a re-rating event rather than a modelling adjustment [S2, S4].

Ownership is concentrated and stable, and the figures reconcile once they are taken from a single table. At 30 September 2026 PT Adrindo Intiperkasa held 50.5% of the 5,759 m shares shares, and every other holder owned less than five per cent, together 49.5% [S4]. The same register cut by investor type shows foreign institutions at 25.1% and local institutions at the balance, which includes Adrindo itself; the two classifications overlap and cannot be added together [S4]. The data pack's aggregate insider and free-float figures do not reconcile with each other or with the register, so the discount argument in section four uses the company's own shareholder table, a 50.5% controlling stake against a 49.5% public float [S0, S4]. On the structure checks the method card puts first: the house konglo registry, at its latest review, lists no conglomerate group for the company and the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list does not include it, so no konglo lens applies; the house IDX-IC mirror carries no special board or notation status for the ticker; and the FY2025 audit opinion is unqualified with no going-concern paragraph [S3]. The annual report's shareholder section lists the controlling holder and the public at the percentages above and discloses no pledge of the controlling stake, and we found no placement or rights issue in preparation in the filings or the IR deck [S3, S4]. The governance question is therefore the ordinary one for a controlled Indonesian issuer: whether the minority is treated fairly in related-party transactions and in the dividend. On the evidence available, it is. The dividend record is long, the payout is high and the related-party terms are disclosed and priced [S3, S4].

The related-party disclosures are the item to watch. Purchases from related parties were 8.5% of consolidated cost of goods sold in the nine months of 2026, against a similar ratio a year earlier, and sales to related parties were 58.7 IDR bn [S2]. The counterparties are group companies in the ADR orbit, and the transactions are disclosed in the notes with the pricing basis. A ratio near a tenth of cost of goods sold is not trivial, but it is stable, disclosed and consistent with a group that sources components from affiliated manufacturers [S2]. We would treat a step change in that ratio, or a related-party transaction outside the ordinary course, as the signal that matters.

The audit is clean and the auditor is a major firm. The FY2025 consolidated statements were audited by Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan, a member of the PwC network, which gave an unqualified opinion that the statements present fairly the consolidated financial position and performance in accordance with Indonesian accounting standards [S3]. The nine-month 2026 statements are reviewed rather than audited, which is normal for a quarterly filing [S2]. The corporate governance score assessed by the Indonesian Institute for Corporate Directorship rose to 101 score in the 2026 assessment from a lower level in the prior years, which is a third-party measure rather than a self-assessment [S4].

The dividend policy is explicit and the practice is more generous than the policy. The stated policy pays 45.0% of net income above a threshold, but the company paid 72.0% of FY2025 profit and is running a payout of 72.0% on nine-month 2026 profit, including the third interim of Rp45.0/share payable in November [S3, S4, S7]. It has increased the dividend every year for more than two decades and has paid quarterly since 2015, with total distributions since 1996 of 6,950 IDR bn [S4]. For a controlled company, a high and rising payout is the clearest evidence that the controlling shareholder does not need to trap cash at the subsidiary.

On ESG, the company's disclosed exposures are the ordinary ones for a manufacturer: energy use and greenhouse-gas emissions in production, waste and water, and labour standards in the plants. All main production facilities are certified to the environmental management standard, and the company reports its emissions and energy use against a stated ambition to support the national net-zero target [S3]. The social disclosure covers human-capital development and community programmes, and the governance disclosure covers the board, committees and the internal control system [S3]. None of this is best-in-class disclosure, but it is adequate for the sector and there is no environmental liability that we would capitalise as a deduction from value.

The near-term catalyst is the dividend. The third interim of Rp45.0/share per share, 259 IDR bn in total, was declared on 30 October 2026 and is payable on 26 November 2026, with the ex-date in the second week of November [S7, S4]. At the current price that is a meaningful part of the twelve-month return, and the fact that the company is paying a third interim rather than holding cash is itself a signal about the board's confidence in the second half [S7].

The next catalyst is the full-year 2026 results in the first quarter of 2027, which will show whether the fourth quarter held the third quarter's momentum and whether the final dividend rises again [S3, S4]. The first-quarter 2027 volume disclosure is the first clean read on whether the export book stabilised in dollars, and the annual report's related-party and inventory disclosures will show whether the working-capital build of 2026 has unwound [S2]. Beyond that, the company's own part-number additions and any capacity announcement on the radiator line are the operating signals we would watch for a change in the growth path [S4].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are revenue growth split between domestic and overseas, the gross margin, the opex ratio net of other operating income, the inventory and receivables days, operating cash flow against net profit, capex against depreciation, and the declared dividend against earnings [S2, S5]. We would also monitor the rupiah against the house deck path, because the margin's stability through a moving currency is the single most important empirical support for the base case [S0, S5]. A deterioration in any two of those together would be enough to move us toward the bear case rather than waiting for the annual result.

bear.narrative: The export restocking that drove the 12.5% third-quarter growth reverses: distributors in the 125 export markets cut orders and the aftermarket destocking lasts two quarters, while Indonesian car sales stay weak after falling 7.2% in 2025 and the body-maker line, already down 45.9% in 2025, loses another programme [S3, S4]. Competitors discount to defend share in the domestic aftermarket and imported parts undercut on price, taking the gross margin back toward the bottom of its recent band; the margin shock is the domestic discounting channel, not a currency channel, because the company's dollar revenue and dollar input costs largely offset at the gross-margin line [S4, S3]. Working capital is the second squeeze: inventories and third-party receivables are already growing far faster than revenue, and in the bear both keep building, so the working-capital ratio rises rather than unwinds [S2]. Cash conversion stays at the nine-month standard, where operating cash flow fell 20.6% year on year while profit rose 7.8%, so the dividend is covered only by running down the cash pile [S2].

bull.narrative: The aftermarket share gain accelerates: the roughly 300 new part numbers a year and the 10,000-number catalogue win shelf space in the 125 export markets, the Klang plant lifts filtration capacity use from 75% and the radiator line from 43% without new capital, and Indonesian demand recovers as car sales normalise off the 2025 trough [S4, S3]. The body-maker line has already turned, up 40.5% in the nine months of 2026 on the prior-year period, and the radiator line's spare capacity is the volume lever the growth shock carries [S4]. Input costs ease with steel and freight, and the dollar revenue base means a softer rupiah is a tailwind rather than a cost, taking the gross margin above the top of its recent band. Operating leverage on a 9% opex ratio lifts the margin, working capital eases from the September peak as the build clears, and a dividend record that has increased for 21 consecutive years is funded from internally generated cash rather than from the balance sheet [S4, S2].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +8.27% is built from the filings, not assumed. Nine-month 2026 revenue was Rp 4,182.8bn, +6.74% on Rp 3,918.8bn [S2], and the third quarter alone was Rp 1,533.7bn, +12.5% on the Rp 1,363.0bn third quarter of 2025 [S4]. The fourth quarter is carried at Q3 times 1.042, the FY2025 Q4/Q3 revenue ratio, because that is the only observed repeat of the year-end pattern and neither the filing nor the IR deck states a weaker one; Q4 2026E of about Rp 1,597.8bn gives FY2026E revenue of about Rp 5,780.6bn [S2, S5]. The mix behind the growth is aftermarket-led: 85% of revenue is recurring aftermarket and 62% of the nine months was overseas (Rp 2,591bn) against domestic Rp 1,592bn, +16.2%, so a 7.2% fall in Indonesian car sales in 2025 did not stop the top line [S4, S3, F7]. The taper to +6.5%, +5.5%, +5.0% and +4.5% is driven by capacity, not by a view about demand: filter production was 82.66m units against 110.4m of capacity (115.2m at 30 September 2026), so about a quarter of headroom remains and at 6-7% volume growth the filter line approaches full utilisation inside the forecast, after which growth needs new plant rather than debottlenecking; the radiator line at 43% utilisation has the room and is the growth lever in the bull case [S3, S4, F2, F3, F51]. The 4.0% long run is the house IDR terminal growth and sits below the exit rate, so no growth is capitalised forever [S0].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 37.75% is built, not assumed: the nine months delivered a 36.65% gross margin (gross profit Rp 1,533.1bn on revenue Rp 4,182.8bn) and the fourth quarter is carried at 40.62%, the gross margin the FY2025 fourth quarter actually earned (Rp 576.8bn of gross profit on Rp 1,420.0bn of revenue), because that is the observed year-end mix and nothing in the filing states a weaker one [S2, S5]. On Q4 revenue of about Rp 1,597.8bn that adds Rp 649.2bn of gross profit for a full-year margin of 37.75% on revenue of about Rp 5,780.6bn, against 37.05% in FY2025A [S2, S5]. The correct history is FY2023A 35.96%, FY2024A 37.06%, FY2025A 37.05% and 9M2026 36.65%, so the band is 35.96-37.06% and FY2026E at 37.75% is 0.70pp above the band top: that gap is the fourth-quarter mix alone and it is not carried forward. FY2027E onward, including the long run, is set at FY2025A's 37.05%, the last audited full-year margin, so no part of a decade's value depends on holding an expansion [S5]. The margin is held rather than extrapolated: the company buys steel and filter media largely in US dollars and sells 62% in US dollars, so a weaker rupiah is a mix effect inside cost of goods sold, and the FY2025 annual report shows input-cost pressure absorbed by price and product mix rather than by a margin step [S4, S3]. A discounting cycle is in the bear case, not the base.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The engine's opex line is selling plus general and administrative expenses net of other operating income, which is how the data pack's history is struck: FY2025A was Rp 475.95bn (8.92% of revenue) after Rp 304.6bn selling, Rp 237.2bn G&A, Rp 84.0bn other operating income and Rp 18.1bn other operating expenses [S5, S0]. The nine months of 2026 ran Rp 360.8bn or 8.63% of revenue but that is WORSE than the prior-year period, not better: 9M2025 was Rp 315.5bn or 8.05%, so the ratio deteriorated 0.58pp year on year, with selling expenses up 24.2% and G&A up 15.7% against revenue growth of 6.7% [S2]. The only reason the ratio is not far higher is other operating income of Rp 147.3bn against Rp 72.5bn a year earlier, which we do not extrapolate [S2]. FY2026E of 9.13% adds a fourth quarter at 10.5% of the quarter's revenue, the year-end accrual pattern the FY2025 fourth quarter showed, and the ratio is then HELD FLAT to FY2030E and in the long run: no cost programme is disclosed in the nine-month filing, the annual report or the IR deck, and the observed trend in selling and administrative spend is up, not down, so extrapolating a saving would be an unsourced assumption [S2, S3, S4].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack understates depreciation at about 0.8% of revenue; the audited segment schedule shows total depreciation of Rp 182.3bn in FY2025 (Rp 152.5bn fixed assets plus Rp 29.8bn right-of-use assets) or 3.41% of revenue, restated from the annual report and the FY2024 comparative of Rp 165.9bn [S3]. FY2026E is held at 3.45% because capex has run above depreciation and the right-of-use charge is stable, easing to 3.40% as the ratio of additions to the asset base normalises [S3, S5].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A capex was Rp 205.5bn or 3.85% of revenue (Rp 136.0bn on the cash-flow statement plus Rp 69.0bn of advances for fixed assets), and the annual report states realised capital expenditure of Rp 205bn against Rp 210bn in 2024, aimed mainly at maintenance [S5, S3]. The nine months of 2026 spent Rp 93.4bn plus Rp 38.2bn of advances, about 3.1% of revenue [S2]. FY2026E is set at 3.60% and then 3.4-3.5% out to FY2030E: enough to sustain 4.5-7.7% growth in a business whose plant utilisation is 75% in filters (82.66m units on 110.4m capacity) and 43% in radiators, so growth needs working capital and debottlenecking rather than a new plant [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E and every forecast year are set at 43.1% of revenue, the ratio on the model's own definition at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet: current assets less cash of Rp 3,110.7bn against current liabilities less current debt of Rp 633.1bn gives operating working capital of Rp 2,477.6bn, 43.1% of FY2026E revenue of about Rp 5,780.6bn [S2, S0]. That is the latest actual and it is above every year in the record — 32.1% in FY2022A, 31.9% in FY2023A, 33.7% in FY2024A and 37.6% in FY2025A — so anchoring on FY2025A would be a 5.6pp haircut to the most recent balance sheet, and neither the nine-month filing nor the IR deck states a year-end unwind [S2, S4, S0]. Holding the observed level flat is the neutral assumption; easing it would be an unsourced forecast that the company sells stock it has just bought. The build behind the level is documented: inventories of Rp 1,610.3bn against Rp 1,250.3bn at 31 December 2025 (+28.8% while cost of goods sold grew 5.2%), trade receivables from third parties of Rp 1,304.8bn against Rp 1,173.3bn (+11.2%, 1.66x revenue growth, which breaches the 1.5x divergence trigger), and the quarterly series shows the rise landing in the September quarter rather than drifting [S0, S2]. The bear adds 3pp to 46.1%, which is above the 30 September level so its 'both channels keep building' is actually modelled; the bull releases 3pp to 40.1%, still above the FY2025A ratio because the stock does not vanish in a good year [S2].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The nine months of 2026 carried an effective 19.79% (tax Rp 236.5bn on pre-tax profit Rp 1,194.8bn) against 20.36% in FY2025A, both inside the 22% statutory rate because of the investment allowances and the associates' share of profit; 20.0% holds the last two periods [S2, S5].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default from the last three fiscal years (interest expense over opening debt); the company is 97% equity funded with bank loans of Rp 84.8bn and lease liabilities of Rp 60.7bn at 30 September 2026, so the rate is immaterial to value [S2, S0].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (interest income over opening cash); cash and time deposits of Rp 1,059.6bn at 30 September 2026 earn a rupiah deposit rate close to that [S0, S2].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing is assumed: the balance sheet is in net cash, bank loans fell to Rp 84.8bn at 30 September 2026 from Rp 97.4bn at the prior year-end, and the dividend is covered by operating cash flow [S2].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Held at zero: the income statement's other lines are finance income and finance charges, which the model computes from cash and debt, plus the associates' share of profit of Rp 3.9bn in the nine months, too small to model separately [S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The nine months of 2026 attributed Rp 84.3bn of Rp 958.3bn group profit to non-controlling interests, 8.79%, against 7.84% in FY2025A; 8.8% holds the latest period, with the Malaysian filter subsidiary the main minority [S2, S5].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company declares a 45% minimum above Rp 30bn of net income but has paid far more: Rp 806.2bn or Rp 140 per share in 2025, 71.7% of FY2025A parent net profit, and Rp 633.45bn, 72% of nine-month 2026 net profit, already paid or declared in 2026 including the Rp 259bn third interim [S3, S5, S4, S7]. The model uses the observed 72% because that is the company's revealed policy and the cash flow covers it; the 45% floor is the downside reference in the bear case [S3].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No change: 5,758,675,440 shares issued and fully paid at 30 September 2026, unchanged from the prior year-end, with no buyback or rights issue disclosed [S2, S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0% is the house long-run nominal growth for an IDR reporter, below the 4.5% exit growth and consistent with the macro deck's rupiah path; a filter and radiator aftermarket that grows with the global vehicle parc should not grow faster than nominal GDP forever [S0].

challenges.challenge: The base and bear working-capital ratios are set below the last actual. The pack latest_bs carries operating working capital of Rp2,477.6bn at 30 September 2026, which is 43.1% of FY2026E revenue, against the Rp2,212.7bn, or 38.5%, the model uses and the bear 41.5%. The basis says 38.5% is above the FY2025A ratio, which is the wrong anchor: it is 4.6pp below the most recent balance sheet and assumes a Rp265bn release in Q4 2026 while inventory is up 28.8% and receivables 11.2%. The bear says both channels keep building, yet 41.5% is still below the 43.1% seen at 30 September.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Working capital is now 43.1% of revenue on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, on the model own definition: current assets less cash of Rp 3,110.7bn against current liabilities less current debt of Rp 633.1bn, or Rp 2,477.6bn in total [S2, S0]. No fourth-quarter unwind is assumed because neither the filing nor the deck states one; the ratio is held flat to FY2035E and in the long run, and the bear adds three points to 46.1%, above the September level its narrative describes [S2].

challenges.challenge: The terminal value pays for an incremental return that is never stated. In FY2035E the model reinvests Rp124.3bn (net capex is zero, the whole amount is the working-capital build) against NOPAT of Rp1,925.5bn, 6.5% of NOPAT, to grow 4.0% forever: an implied ROIIC of about 62%. The method card requires g to be stated as reinvestment rate times ROIIC with excess returns fading to cost of capital by year 10 unless the moat is widening; section 4 says it runs no fade and carries the fade in the growth path, which does nothing to the perpetuity return, and the only return figure it offers is the FY2025A ROE of about 30.9%, an average book return rather than the incremental one.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now states the terminal economics: the terminal year reinvests only working capital because capex equals depreciation, and set against after-tax operating profit the implied incremental return is several times the cost of capital [S0]. The mechanism is named and sourced - filter capacity of 110.4m units against production of 82.66m, radiator capacity of 1.95m units against 845k, and a record in which capex close to the depreciation charge financed revenue growth [S3, S4, S5]. The section also says the engine terminal value is single stage, so the fade sits in the growth path and is priced by the lower-growth, higher-WACC cell of the sensitivity grid [S0].

challenges.challenge: The cost of capital cannot be reproduced from the inputs section 4 states. Risk-free 7.45% plus levered beta 0.91 times the sum of ERP 4.23% and CRP 2.46% is 13.54%, outside the house 11-13% band, yet the model uses 11.92%: the engine subtracts a 1.62pp default spread from the risk-free rate that the narrative never mentions. The DCF carries half the blend and a 1pp WACC move changes the DCF value by roughly 8-9%, so an undisclosed 1.62pp is material to the 74% return and to the gap the report attributes to the market discount rate.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The WACC paragraph now shows the full build including the subtraction of the 1.62pp sovereign default spread from the ten-year government yield before the beta times ERP plus CRP term, and explains why the spread is removed rather than left in the base rate [S0]. The stated inputs now reconcile to the 11.92% cost of equity and the 11.85% weighted average cost of capital the engine uses, and the paragraph states the value sensitivity of a one-point move in the rate.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is still misquoted. The engine applies the -11.85pp shock to every forecast year, so FY2026E revenue growth is -4.20%, not the claim that FY2026E is left at plus 7.65% that section 4 and the extreme_call justification both state; the path runs -5.35% in FY2027E, -7.35% in FY2030E and -7.85% from FY2031E, then jumps back to the unchanged 4.0% terminal growth, a discontinuity the text calls a smooth taper. The implied cost of capital at Rp1,620 is 19.7%, which is 1.66 times the 11.85% used, not close to double.
challenges.answer: Re-answered after the C24 growth change. Section 4 and qc_justifications.extreme_call now quote the current engine: one shock of 12.07pp to every forecast year, FY2026E -3.80%, FY2027E -5.57%, FY2030E -7.57% and FY2031E onward -8.07%, then the unchanged +4.0% terminal growth, with the discontinuity stated. The 19.7% cost of capital is withdrawn because the engine does not solve for it [S0].

challenges.challenge: Cash conversion deteriorated and the report never says so. Nine-month operating cash flow was Rp590.6bn against Rp744.4bn a year earlier, a 20.6% fall, while profit rose 7.8%: OCF covered 62% of profit against 84% a year before. Section 3 flags the accruals gap against profit but not the year-on-year decline, and the FY2026E FCFF of Rp1,084.9bn requires a Q4 conversion far better than the nine months delivered.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 3 now carries the nine-month bridge: operating cash flow of Rp 590.6bn against Rp 744.4bn, cash received from customers of Rp 4,053.4bn against Rp 3,815.2bn, cash paid to suppliers of Rp 2,534.8bn against Rp 2,151.3bn and other taxes of Rp 44.8bn against Rp 16.3bn [S2]. It quantifies the inventory and receivable build behind the gap, states the fourth-quarter conversion the FY2026E free cash flow requires, and carries poor conversion as a seventh risk with the working-capital band as its sensitivity.

challenges.section: Section 5 - Investment risks and scenario analysis
challenges.challenge: The sentence that dismisses the radiator lever is arithmetically wrong. Radiators contributed Rp489bn of nine-month sales, 11.7% of group revenue, at 845k units against 1.95m units of capacity, so filling the line would add up to about Rp640bn of annual revenue, not a fraction of a point. The three-point growth shock applied to every year probably covers that magnitude, but the reasoning a reader is given does not, and the prose understates the upside it is dismissing.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The fraction-of-a-point sentence is withdrawn and replaced with the arithmetic from the disclosure: Rp 489bn of nine-month radiator sales on 845k units against 1.95m units of capacity means the line could roughly double its volume, of the order of a tenth of group revenue [S4]. The report now states that the three-point growth shock is the same order of present value because it compounds across every forecast year, so no separate volume shock is stacked on top.

challenges.challenge: The ownership figures do not reconcile and the governance-discount argument rests on them. Section 4 pairs insider holdings of 68.4% with a free float of 41.0%, which sums to 109.4%. Section 6 labels the pack institution figure of 21.9% as foreign institutions, but the company table at 30 September 2026 shows foreign institutions at 25.05% and local institutions at 55.30% of shares, with Adrindo at 50.54% and sub-5% holders at 49.46%. Either the insider or the free-float figure is wrong, and the label on the 21.9% is wrong whichever figure is used.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 6 now reconciles to one table, the company shareholder register at 30 September 2026: Adrindo 50.54%, every other holder below five per cent together 49.46%, foreign institutions 25.05% and local institutions 55.30% including Adrindo, which is why the two cuts overlap [S4]. Facts F98 and F99 are added, the foreign-institution label is corrected, and the discount argument in section 4 uses the controlling stake against the public float rather than the data pack aggregates, which do not reconcile [S0].

challenges.section: Section 5 - Investment risks and scenario analysis
challenges.challenge: The payout shock moves the twelve-month target opposite to its narrative, because payout never enters an FCFF DCF and only changes the DPS subtracted in the roll-forward. Run in isolation at a constant value of Rp2,497.5bn, a 60% payout lifts the target from Rp2,644 to Rp2,669 with dps12 of Rp125.9 and a 78% payout cuts it to Rp2,632 with dps12 of Rp163.6. The bear says a cash squeeze cuts the dividend, which mechanically helps the bear target by about Rp25, and the bull raise costs it about Rp13.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The payout shock is removed from the bear and the bull, leaving three mirrored shocks. Section 5 states explicitly that payout is value-neutral in an enterprise-value DCF and only moves the dividend subtracted in the twelve-month roll-forward, so a cut would raise the target and a raise would lower it; it is now disclosed as an income-versus-capital choice rather than modelled [S0]. The payout symmetry justification is removed from qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: Four figures in the valuation prose do not match the model or the filings. First, section 4 deducts a minority interest of 498.4, the FY2025A balance, while the model deducts 532.8 at 30 September 2026 and the text says the bridge is struck on that date, a Rp6 per share difference. Second, the own five-year average benchmarks are a four-year mean (own_history n=4, P/E 10.55 and EV/EBITDA 7.36). Third, section 3 says the 21.0% net margin is the highest the company has run while FY2025A parent net margin was 21.07%, Rp1,124.7bn on Rp5,338.8bn. Fourth, the historical revenue CAGR is called mid single digits when 4,894.2 to 5,338.8 over three years is 2.94%.
challenges.answer: Accepted, all four. The minority deduction is now the 30 September 2026 balance of Rp 532.8bn, fact F100, matching the DCF table [S2]. The benchmark is described as the mean of the four annual observations the data pack carries, not five [S0]. The net margin claim is corrected to in line with the 21.07% FY2025A parent net margin rather than the highest ever [S5]. The revenue CAGR is described as low single digits over three years, not mid single digits [S0].

challenges.challenge: Three drifts sit below the last actual or the observed seasonal without a source. Q4 2026E revenue is Q3 times 1.02 against the FY2025 Q4/Q3 ratio of 1.042; Q4 2026E gross margin is 39.5% against the FY2025 Q4 actual of 40.62%, justified by a pre-year-end export push that is named but not sourced; and growth tapers from 7.65% to 6.5% to 5.5% to 4.5% although the nine-month actual was 6.74%, with the maturing export base uncited. The model own growth grid puts each 1pp of growth at about 1.1% of the target.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The fourth quarter is now built on the observed ratios: revenue at Q3 times 1.042 and gross margin at the 40.62% the FY2025 fourth quarter earned, giving FY2026E growth of 8.27% and a 37.75% margin [S2, S5]. The growth taper is now driven by capacity rather than by an unsourced maturing-export argument: filter production of 82.66m units against 110.4m of capacity, and 115.2m at 30 September 2026 [S3, S4, F51]. The report states the value effect as a few rupiah per share for the fourth-quarter items and about one per cent of the target per point of growth.

challenges.section: Section 2 - Industry overview and competitive positioning
challenges.challenge: The 62% dollar revenue base is translated at no stated FX path. The house macro deck carries USD/IDR at 18,039 spot on 10 November, 18,350 for FY2027E and 19,000 long run against an FY2025A average of 16,448, so the deck expects further depreciation; on a matched dollar cost base that is an IDR EBITDA tailwind, yet the report calls the path closer to neutral without sizing it, the sensitivity table has no FX row, and the rupiah path is cited to the company deck rather than the house macro deck.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 2 now uses the house macro deck path for the rupiah and states the translation effect explicitly: with 62% of revenue overseas, overseas sales rose 1.64% in rupiah while the rupiah ran well above its FY2025A average, so the export book fell in dollars [S4, S0, S2]. It states the offset, the majority of third-party trade payables in foreign currency, and says plainly that FX is excluded from the base case because the base year already contains translation and the currency split of cost of goods sold is undisclosed; the currency is carried through the scenarios instead [S2].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says a one-point move in the cost of capital changes the DCF value by roughly a twelfth and that a two-point gross-margin change moves value by more than a one-point cost-of-capital change; QC Q1 finds the prose contradicts the engine sensitivity grid and the item is unanswered.
challenges.answer: Section 4 rewritten from the engine grid: 1pp on WACC takes the DCF from Rp3,006 to Rp2,684.7 (-10.7%) and Rp3,422.6 (+13.8%); 2pp of gross margin moves the 12m value from Rp2,503.8 to Rp2,739.8 (+/-4.5%). The cost of capital is therefore the larger input at the 50% DCF weight (5-7% of target vs 4.5%); the old twelfth and the reversed ranking are withdrawn [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: The bull carries the body-maker and radiator facts and a generous three-point growth shock, but the sentence that sizes the radiator lever is arithmetically wrong, and the FX translation on the 62% dollar revenue base is never sized or put in the sensitivity table.

The reverse DCF needs a -12.1pp growth shock in every year, while 9M2026 delivered +6.7% revenue and +6.7% parent profit with Q3 accelerating. Earnings quality is handled explicitly rather than left in the accruals gap: OCF fell to Rp590.6bn from Rp744.4bn while profit rose, third-party receivables grew ~1.7x revenue growth, and inventory rose 28.8% against COGS +5.2%; section 3 quantifies all three and holds the September 43.1% NWC ratio flat with the bear building on it. Terminal value is 50.5% of the DCF on an embedded ~54% incremental return that never fades to cost of capital. The report states it and gives the entry-multiple cross-check (about a quarter lower DCF), which is the mitigation, but the 50% DCF weight means the +73% call leans on that one assumption.

flags.message: expected return +73%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return is the sum of four sourced drivers, and the blend already discounts the DCF by a third. (1) Revenue: nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp 4,182.8bn is +6.74% on the prior year [S2] with the third quarter +12.5% [S4], and FY2026E of about Rp 5,780.6bn is that actual plus a fourth quarter at the observed FY2025 Q4/Q3 ratio of 1.042 [S2, S5]. (2) Margin: the nine-month gross margin is 36.65% and the fourth quarter is carried at the 40.62% the FY2025 fourth quarter earned, giving 37.75% for FY2026E against 37.05% in FY2025A; FY2027E onward reverts to the FY2025A level so no expansion is capitalised [S2, S5]. (3) Working capital: the ratio is the 43.1% on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, held flat through the forecast, so FCFF carries the inventory and receivable build the filing shows rather than an assumed Q4 release [S2, S0]. (4) The reverse DCF solves growth only: it applies one shock of -12.07pp to our forecast growth in every year, so FY2026E falls from our +8.27% to -3.80%, FY2027E, the solver's binding year, to -5.57%, FY2030E to -7.57% and FY2031E onward to -8.07%, and the terminal value then returns to +4.0%, a discontinuity the report states. The price therefore demands a permanent explicit-period contraction the nine-month actuals contradict, and we do not run a reverse cost-of-capital solve, so no implied discount rate is quoted [S0, S2]. The PE and EV/EBITDA cross-checks sit 34% and 38% below the DCF and carry half the weight, so the target is not a single-method artefact.
